Inverse Gaussian Log-CDF Derivatives

Source: R/cdf_normal_higher.R
distrib_grad_cdf.InvGauss1Distrib.Rd

Returns the derivatives in closed form at every order from one to four. The inverse Gaussian's distribution function is elementary, $$F(q) = \Phi(a) + e^{c}\,\Phi(b), \qquad a = \frac{q/\mu - 1}{\sqrt{\phi q}}, \quad b = -\frac{q/\mu + 1}{\sqrt{\phi q}}, \quad c = \frac{2}{\phi\mu},$$ so it can simply be differentiated. This page's four registrations are made together by register_phi_terms_cdf().

Arguments

distrib

An InvGauss1Distrib object, from invgauss1_distrib().

q

A numeric vector of quantiles, positive.

theta

A named list with components mu (positive) and phi (positive); each is a numeric vector of length 1 or n.

lower.tail

A single logical, TRUE by default; TRUE selects the lower tail and FALSE the upper tail.

log

A single logical, TRUE by default; TRUE selects the derivatives of the log probability and FALSE those of the probability.

...

Unused, and accepted so that the signature matches the generic's.

Value

A named list of numeric vectors of the requested order, keyed as deriv_names(distrib@params, order): two components for the gradient, three for the Hessian, four at order 3 and five at order 4.

Separable partial derivatives

Each of \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) is a product of a function of the mean and a function of the dispersion, so every mixed partial is a product of two one-variable derivatives. The two terms are then a Leibniz split between the weight and the tail, which phi_terms_cdf_deriv_k() runs on the package's own partition enumeration.

Overflow of the weight

\(e^{c}\) overflows to Inf once \(c = 2/(\phi\mu)\) exceeds about 709; the exponent is 2000 at \(\mu = 0.01\), \(\phi = 0.1\). Where it overflows, \(\Phi(b)\) underflows, and the product is finite. The weight and the tail are therefore combined as exp(c + pnorm(b, log.p = TRUE)).

Accuracy

The derivatives are closed forms. A product stencil on the same distribution function loses accuracy as the order grows, so the family registers all four orders.

Notation

\(\mu > 0\) is the mean, \(\phi > 0\) the dispersion, \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function and \(F\) the inverse Gaussian's.

See also

phi_terms_cdf_deriv_k() for the construction; register_phi_terms_cdf(), which makes the four registrations; distrib_grad_cdf.EnetDistrib(), the other family of this shape; invgauss1_distrib().

Examples

d <- invgauss1_distrib()
q <- c(0.5, 2, 5)
th <- list(mu = 2, phi = 0.5)

# The gradient is compared with a central difference of the cdf, which
# shares no arithmetic.
fd <- numerical_cdf_deriv(d, q, th, order = 1)
max(abs(unlist(distrib_grad_cdf(d, q, th, log = FALSE)) / unlist(fd) - 1))
#> [1] 9.956747e-11

# The gradient is finite although the weight overflows: exp(2 / (phi mu))
# is Inf here.
exp(2 / (0.01 * 0.1))
#> [1] Inf
distrib_grad_cdf(d, 0.02, list(mu = 0.01, phi = 0.1), log = FALSE)
#> $mu
#> [1] -3.174073e-106
#> 
#> $phi
#> [1] -7.929894e-108
#>
